channel.title: Regency House Assisted Living: Senior Care News
channel.description: Senior housing, senior care and caregiving news from trusted publishers, gathered by our team for families in Hixson and the Chattanooga area. The summaries are ours; the full stories belong to their publishers.

item.title: IRS raises the 2027 limits on deductible long-term care insurance premiums; the cap for people over 70 is $6,290
item.description: The IRS has published its 2027 inflation adjustments, and the American Association for Long-Term Care Insurance summarizes what they mean for policyholders. The amount of a qualified long-term care insurance premium that can count as a medical expense rises by age band, topping out at $6,290 a year for people over 70, up from $6,200 in 2026; the cap is $5,030 for ages 61 to 70. The per-day benefit that can be received tax-free rises to $445. The association notes that the deduction only helps people who itemize and whose medical expenses clear the usual threshold, and that many hybrid life policies with care riders do not qualify. Why it matters: If a parent pays long-term care premiums, the 2027 numbers belong in next year's tax planning; the policy's own benefit terms still decide what it pays toward assisted living.

item.title: Direct care job vacancies are easing, survey finds, but assisted living still has more openings than two years ago
item.description: McKnight's Senior Living reports on a new survey of direct care employers showing that the share of unfilled healthcare positions fell to about 14 percent between 2024 and 2026, helped by recruiting and retention programs adopted after the pandemic. Assisted living was the exception on volume: openings there rose about 6 percent over the same period, and entry-level roles such as certified nursing assistants made up roughly 44 percent of the vacancies. The piece pairs the survey with the recently released Activated Insights workforce index, which found assisted living turnover falling to about 72 percent after peaking above 84 percent in late 2024. Why it matters: Staffing is the question behind every tour; ask how long the caregivers you meet have been there and how open shifts are covered.

item.title: CDC: adults 75 and older should get a single RSV vaccine dose, and it does not need to be repeated each year
item.description: The CDC's adult guidance recommends one dose of RSV vaccine for everyone 75 and older and for adults 50 to 74 who are at higher risk of severe illness, a group that includes people with chronic heart or lung disease, diabetes, kidney disease and those living in nursing homes or other group settings. Unlike the flu shot, the RSV vaccine is not an annual vaccine, so someone who has already had a dose does not need another this season. RSV sends tens of thousands of older adults to the hospital each winter, and the CDC says the best time to get the shot is late summer or early fall, though it can be given any time during the season. Why it matters: Check whether a parent has ever had the RSV shot; if not, it is a one-time errand worth asking the pharmacy or doctor about before the holidays.

item.title: Senior living demand keeps outrunning new construction; a new Argentum and NIC MAP report points to costs and margins
item.description: Senior Housing News reports on a new analysis from Argentum and NIC MAP that tries to explain why so few senior living communities are being built even as occupancy climbs. Construction starts fell to about 10,000 units in 2025 while demand kept rising. The report's authors argue that the industry measures demand well, through occupancy, move-ins and rates, but has little shared data on what communities spend and why operating costs have changed since 2020, and that thin margins rather than weak demand are what keep new projects from getting financed. The analysis is meant to give operators and lenders a common picture of expenses. Why it matters: Few new communities are opening, so a family that finds a good fit should expect waiting lists and start the conversation early rather than wait for a new building.

item.title: Medicare Part B premium rises to $209.40 a month in 2027, a smaller increase than the Social Security raise
item.description: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced on November 17 that the standard Medicare Part B premium will be $209.40 a month in 2027, up $6.50 from $202.90 this year, and that the annual Part B deductible rises from $283 to $292. The premium is deducted from most Social Security checks, so it takes a bite out of the 3.6 percent cost-of-living increase arriving in January; this year the premium increase is smaller than the raise, which has not happened since 2023. People with higher incomes pay an income-related surcharge on top of the standard amount. Beneficiaries will see their exact 2027 deduction in the Social Security notice mailed in December. Why it matters: For a parent on a fixed income, the net January check is the number to budget care around; the December notice shows it.

item.title: AARP's checklist for judging whether an older parent needs more help at home
item.description: AARP's caregiving guide lists the signs relatives can check during a visit when they wonder whether a parent is still managing alone. It covers changes in appearance and hygiene, unexplained weight loss, bruises or burns that may come from struggling with cookware, expired food in the refrigerator, unopened mail and late bills, new dents on the car, missed or unfilled prescriptions, and pulling back from friends and hobbies. The guide suggests comparing notes with siblings, using video calls between visits to notice gradual change, and asking the parent what help they would accept rather than announcing a plan. Why it matters: Thanksgiving is often the first long visit of the year; a shared checklist turns vague worry into specific things a family can act on together.

item.title: Virginia audit finds only 18 percent of older residents can afford assisted living, urges stronger oversight
item.description: Virginia's legislative audit office reviewed the state's assisted living sector and reported that only about 18 percent of older Virginians have enough income to afford the average rate in their region, with the share ranging from roughly a third in some northern suburbs to single digits in the rural southwest. The review also recommended tighter state oversight and clearer staffing standards, while the state's provider association cautioned that new mandates would raise operating costs. The report is one of the most detailed looks any state has taken at who can and cannot pay for assisted living. Why it matters: Affordability and staffing standards vary widely by state and region, so families should ask any community how its rate is set and how it is staffed, not assume a national average applies.

item.title: New trial asks whether adults over 70 without heart disease can stop statins; researchers say decide with your doctor
item.description: A European trial presented at the American Heart Association's annual meeting followed about 1,900 adults aged 70 and older who took a statin only to prevent a first heart attack or stroke and who had at least two other chronic conditions. Over roughly two years, those who stopped the drug met the study's safety threshold, though a small increase in cardiovascular events was observed and the authors said the findings do not support a blanket recommendation to stop. People with existing heart disease were not included. Researchers framed the result as a reason for an individual conversation between an older patient and their clinician about which medications still serve a purpose. Why it matters: Medication reviews matter for older adults; this is a question to raise with a doctor, not a change to make on your own.

item.title: Free 'In the Heart of Hixson' concert at North River Civic Center on Friday, November 20
item.description: The City of Chattanooga's Department of Community Development is inviting residents to a free concert featuring Chattanooga Metro Musicians at the North River Civic Center in Hixson on Friday, November 20, at 7 p.m. The civic center's In the Heart of Hixson series brings local musicians and ensembles to the neighborhood on select Friday evenings through the winter, with hour-long, family-friendly performances and no ticket required. The center is on Executive Drive off Hixson Pike, a short drive from most of the neighborhood. Why it matters: A free, close-to-home evening out is an easy way for families to include an older relative who no longer drives after dark.

item.title: Family caregivers now spend about 60 percent more out of pocket than five years ago, AARP study finds
item.description: NPR discussed a new AARP survey of more than 2,500 family caregivers that puts their average out-of-pocket spending at about $11,500 a year, roughly 60 percent higher than five years ago. Food, housing and medical costs make up the largest share, and about half of caregivers say they have cut savings, worked extra hours or drawn on retirement money to cover it. Caregivers of someone with dementia spend more. The segment also walks through what paid help costs nationally, from hourly home care to adult day programs and residential care, and why families often reach a point where caring at home no longer adds up. Why it matters: If caregiving costs are climbing at home, it is worth comparing the full monthly picture against a residential option before a crisis forces the decision.

item.title: UTC's MobileMOC clinic earns national age-friendly recognition for bringing care to seniors across Southeast Tennessee
item.description: The University of Tennessee at Chattanooga says its MobileMOC program has been recognized as a participant in the national Age-Friendly Health Systems movement, and its care model has been published in NEJM Catalyst. MobileMOC is a mobile primary care and wellness clinic run by UTC's nursing program that visits senior centers and community sites across the ten-county district served by the Southeast Tennessee Area Agency on Aging and Disability, which includes Hamilton County. It serves adults 62 and older and their caregivers regardless of insurance, funded by a Tennessee Department of Health grant, and gives UTC students hands-on training with older patients. Why it matters: A free, mobile option for check-ups and wellness screenings that older adults in Hixson and the surrounding counties can reach at a local senior center.

item.title: Is your Medicare Advantage plan ending in 2027? Hundreds of counties lose plans, and enrollment closes December 7
item.description: NPR reports that many Medicare Advantage plans will not be offered in 2027, and that in 193 counties nationwide no Advantage plan is available at all, up from about 120 counties a year earlier according to a KFF analysis. Insurers can also cap enrollment on plans they keep, so waiting can mean a preferred plan is already full. Anyone whose plan is closing should have received a letter in early October. Open enrollment runs through December 7, and Medicare's online Plan Finder lets families compare what is still offered in their county. People whose plan is discontinued get an extra window into early 2027 to choose a new one. Why it matters: If an older parent is on a Medicare Advantage plan, check the October letter and the Plan Finder before December 7 so coverage does not lapse on January 1.

item.title: Georgia opens its first PACE center, a sign the all-inclusive care program for frail seniors keeps spreading in the Southeast
item.description: Georgia's first Program of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly center opened in Savannah on November 10 and is now enrolling, WTOC reports. PACE is a Medicare and Medicaid program for people 55 and older who qualify for a nursing home level of care but can live safely at home or in the community with support. A PACE team coordinates medical care, therapy, medications, transportation and day services under one plan, and the program pays for that care. Georgia passed its PACE law in 2024 and awarded start-up grants to three organizations; this is the first site to open. Tennessee already has PACE programs, and Regency House accepts PACE participants. Why it matters: PACE can cover the care side for a frail parent who qualifies, which changes the math for families comparing home, assisted living and nursing home options.

item.title: November is Alzheimer's Awareness and Family Caregivers Month: how to support a caregiver through the holidays
item.description: The Alzheimer's Association marks November as both National Alzheimer's Disease Awareness Month and National Family Caregivers Month. Its page for the month focuses on the people doing the caring and lists concrete ways relatives and friends can lighten the load during the holidays: take over cooking, cleaning or gift shopping, offer to host the family gathering, and set a standing time each week to sit with the person who has dementia so the main caregiver can rest. The association also points caregivers to its 24-hour helpline and local support groups, including those in the Chattanooga area. Why it matters: If someone in your family is the primary caregiver, the most useful holiday gift is scheduled, dependable time off.

item.title: Families use AI to research senior living, but the tour still decides it, U.S. News survey finds
item.description: U.S. News & World Report surveyed about 500 adults who had recently moved a relative into senior living or were actively searching. Most now use AI tools and online search to build a shortlist of communities, but the survey found that the in-person visit and the people a family meets on tour day are what settle the final choice. Respondents still value a clear written explanation of services, a chance to talk with current residents and staff, and a community that answers questions directly. Half of those surveyed had completed a move in 2025 or 2026 and half were in the middle of a search. Why it matters: Online research narrows the list, but a family should still plan to visit, ask questions in person and see a meal or activity before deciding.

item.title: Why mid-priced senior living stays scarce: operators say capital and scale, not ideas, are the obstacle
item.description: Senior Housing News reports on a National Investment Center panel about housing for older adults who earn too much for subsidized programs but struggle with market-rate senior living. Panelists said the industry does not lack workable ideas. Communities that serve this group keep costs down by offering a simpler menu of services and fewer customization options. What holds back growth is financing and the ability to operate at scale, since lenders and investors still favor higher-end projects. The piece reflects a wider trend in the trade press this fall: new construction is leaning upscale while mid-priced supply grows slowly. Why it matters: Families shopping for assisted living in 2026 are choosing from a market with little new mid-priced supply, so starting the search early and asking what services are included matters more than ever.

item.title: Latest national cost survey: assisted living rates rose about 5 percent, with wide differences by state
item.description: CareScout's annual Cost of Care Survey, the long-running national benchmark formerly published by Genworth, collected more than 25,000 provider rates between July and November 2025. Its 2026 release puts the national median for an assisted living community at about $6,200 a month, roughly 5 percent higher than the year before. Trade coverage noted that long-term care cost growth slowed in 2025 after several years of steep increases. The survey also shows large differences between states and between care settings, and CareScout cautions that actual costs depend on a person's care needs, local availability and the services included. Why it matters: A national median is only a starting point; families should ask any community for a written breakdown of what its monthly rate includes before comparing options.

item.title: City of Chattanooga property tax freeze for homeowners 65 and older: 2026 applications open, help sessions at community centers
item.description: The City of Chattanooga has opened its 2026 property tax freeze application for homeowners who are 65 or older and meet the program's income limit. The freeze locks the city portion of the property tax bill at its current amount; it does not apply to Hamilton County taxes, which the county commission is considering separately. The application deadline is April 5, 2027. City staff offer in-person help by appointment at City Hall and at several community centers, including a Hixson location, on dates listed in the city's senior programs appointment calendar. Questions go to the city's tax relief line at (423) 643-7274 or taxrelief@chattanooga.gov. Why it matters: An older parent still living at home in Chattanooga may qualify for a lower city tax bill, and the application help sessions are a practical errand for a family member to handle this winter.

item.title: Social Security explains new Medicare eligibility rules; some enrollees must confirm status before February 1
item.description: The Social Security Administration issued a notice on November 10 describing how a 2025 federal law changes who can be enrolled in Medicare. Eligibility is limited to U.S. citizens and nationals, lawful permanent residents, Cuban and Haitian entrants, and certain Compact of Free Association migrants. People already enrolled whose status cannot be confirmed in federal records will receive a letter and have until February 1, 2027, to document their eligibility or lose Medicare coverage. The agency says Social Security retirement, disability and survivor benefit rules are not affected by the change. Why it matters: If a parent receives a letter about Medicare eligibility, respond before the deadline and ask a benefits counselor for help; a coverage gap would hit at the worst time.

item.title: Chattanooga's 2026 Walk to End Alzheimer's draws families to Erlanger Park
item.description: Hundreds of Chattanooga-area residents gathered at Erlanger Park on Saturday, November 7, for the city's 2026 Walk to End Alzheimer's, the Alzheimer's Association's annual fundraiser for research, care and support programs. Walkers carried the association's colored flowers that mark their connection to the disease: caregivers, people living with it, those who have lost someone, and supporters. Money raised stays partly local, funding the association's 24-hour helpline, support groups and education programs available to families across Hamilton County. Why it matters: The Alzheimer's Association's local chapter runs free support groups and a 24-hour helpline that Chattanooga families can use year-round, not just on walk day.
